activities.anchor: The format's history explains its quirks
activities.caption: scrub a thousand years of design decisions
activities.name: rnTimeline

events.title: Guido draws lines
events.text: Guido of Arezzo puts the squiggles on lines: height becomes pitch — his claim that learning time fell from ten years to two is the first recorded usability study.

events.title: Petrucci prints
events.text: The printing press (Venice) makes music mass-reproducible; mensural notation has already fixed rhythm.

events.title: Barlines arrive
events.text: The staff notates only what a singer can remember — it needed centuries to accept barlines as standard furniture.

events.title: Tempo marks arrive
events.text: Tempo marks, then dynamics, join the page — the expressive layer completes the modern system.

activities.anchor: so the rest of the ladder is defined
activities.caption: pair each clef with the line it pins
activities.name: rnClefMatch

config.prompt: A clef pins one line to one note. Pair each clef with what it pins:

pairs.right: dots the fourth line as the F below middle C
pins middle C itself — for the viola
pins middle C for cello and the bassoon's high range
the hinge — one ledger line between the staves, shared by both clefs

config.why: The staff is optimised for vocal ranges — hence many clefs, so each voice type stays on the staff without a rain of ledger lines.

activities.anchor: Durations are encoded as shapes that halve
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the bar that does not add up
activities.name: rnBarSpot

config.prompt: A student's bar of 4/4 contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: A whole note = 4 beats in 4/4; a half = 2; a quarter = 1; an eighth = ½.
A dot adds half again: a dotted half = 3 beats.
A tie joins notes across beats or barlines into one held sound.
The worked bar: quarter rest (1) + two beamed eighths (½ + ½) + dotted quarter (1½) + an eighth (½) = 3 beats.
config.correction: The bar sums to exactly 4 beats: 1 + ½ + ½ + 1½ + ½ = 4 — chunky fractions that groove like a backbeat.
config.why: The shapes are fractions, and reading rhythm is doing that fraction arithmetic at sight.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — decoding the signature
activities.name: rnKeyCloze

config.text: One sharp (F♯) on the staff means every F is sharp — the key of %%0%% or %%1%% — and for sharp keys the decoding rule is: a semitone above the %%2%% is the major key.
config.hint: One sharp; two possible homes; the rule reads the last sharp in the F♯ C♯ G♯ order.

activities.caption: true or false — spelling is grammar
activities.name: rnEnhJudge

statements.s: In F♯ major the leading tone is spelled E♯, not F.
statements.why: F would misname the scale degree — and the order of sharps marches through exactly that E♯.

statements.s: E♯ and C♭ do not exist because on the keyboard they look like F and B.
statements.why: The keyboard hides the spelling; the key signature is where it lives.

statements.s: The letter names are grammar, not acoustics.
statements.why: F♯ rising 'to' G tells the reader a direction; G♭ falling 'to' F another.

statements.s: F♯ and G♭ are two different keys on the keyboard.
statements.why: They name the same keys — that is enharmonic spelling.

activities.caption: file each interval by the flavour it carries
activities.name: rnFlavourBuckets

config.prompt: Hearing the flavours — file each interval:
config.why: Count letter-steps first, then measure semitones for the quality — the drill that makes intervals practical.

activities.anchor: sounds a fixed distance from what is written
activities.caption: walk the decision — writing for a transposing player
activities.name: rnTransposeBranch

config.root: Concert C must sound. The player's instrument transposes — what do you write?

start.text: Which player are you writing for?

choices.label: A horn in F
choices.feedback: The horn sounds a perfect fifth below what is written.

choices.label: A flute or violin (C instrument)
choices.feedback: Concert pitch scores are the reference everyone transposes from.

choices.label: Either — just write C and let them transpose at sight
choices.feedback: The page and the room would disagree by accident — composers double-check transpositions.

horn.text: Write G: the horn in F sounds a perfect fifth below its written note — one fingering map per player is the return; score arithmetic is the price.

concert.text: Write C as it sounds: C instruments like flute, violin and piano are the reference everyone transposes from.

sight.text: Ensemble reading is transposition arithmetic done at speed — the convention exists so players learn fingerings once, not so they can transpose on the fly.

config.why: History and habit: doubling on a differently-sized instrument of the same family (B♭ clarinet to A clarinet) changes only the key signature, not the fingers.

activities.anchor: Above the grid lives everything the composer refused to leave to chance
activities.caption: stack the dynamics soft to loud
activities.name: rnDynamicsOrder

config.prompt: The dynamic markings, from softest to loudest:
config.why: Dynamics set loudness as a relative scale, with the hairpins of crescendo and diminuendo between them — the gaps are where interpretation lives.
